meta.title: KEEP YOUR BRAIN ALIVE
meta.author: Lawrence C. Katz, Ph.D. & Manning Rubin

parts.title: KEEP YOUR BRAIN ALIVE: An Introduction to Neurobics
parts.body: This book, Keep Your Brain Alive, by Lawrence C. Katz and Manning Rubin, introduces Neurobics, a new form of brain exercise designed to prevent memory loss and increase mental fitness. Published by Workman Publishing Company in 1999, it emphasizes that many negative myths about the aging brain are untrue. The authors argue that similar to physical health, mental health can be maintained and enhanced through specific strategies. Neurobics is presented as a scientifically-backed approach that utilizes the five senses in novel ways to stimulate new neural activity patterns and create more connections between different brain areas, leading to the production of neurotrophins, natural brain nutrients that strengthen nerve cells and their dendrites. Unlike traditional brain exercises, Neurobics focuses on multisensory associations to build a stronger memory network, making the brain more agile and flexible overall.

parts.title: Our Underused Senses
parts.body: Our senses are key to how our brain interacts with the world. We mostly rely on sight and hearing, but our other senses like smell, taste, and touch are often underused. When we close our eyes, our world changes drastically, and touch becomes very important, making our brain go into high alert. The modern world, with its plastic packaging and deodorized items, reduces the demands on our senses of touch and smell. Historically, smell was crucial for survival and memory, and it's the only sense with direct connections to parts of the brain involved in emotions and memories. This is why certain smells can trigger strong emotional responses. Emotions themselves are a "sixth sense" for the brain, and studies show that memory is tied to emotional context. Social interactions are vital for engaging emotions and promoting non-routine activities, which keep the brain healthy, especially as we age. Modern life, with its conveniences and increased isolation, has reduced these important sensory and social engagements. Engaging all senses, including emotional and social ones, is essential for a healthy brain.

parts.title: AT MEALTIMES
parts.body: This section of the text, titled "KEEP YOUR BRAIN ALIVE AT MEALTIMES," highlights how taste is deeply connected to social activity and emotional memory. The author, Diane Ackerman, notes that meals often involve sharing daily events with family and are linked to special occasions, religious rituals, holidays, and celebrations. This makes the dining experience much more than just eating. The text emphasizes that during meals, all our senses—visual, olfactory (smell), tactile (touch), taste, and even our emotional/pleasure systems—are actively engaged. This rich multisensory involvement contributes significantly to the experience and the lasting memories we form around food.

parts.title: KEEP YOUR BRAIN ALIVE: AT MEALTIMES
parts.body: To keep your brain alive, engage in activities that challenge your mind. Meals, for example, offer a great opportunity to do this. Instead of predictable, repetitive meals, make mealtimes social by removing distractions like newspapers or TV, and focusing on the food and company. This engages your senses and promotes brain-healthy interactions. You can also share a meal in silence to heighten your awareness of tastes, textures, and sounds, or switch seats at the table to challenge ingrained associations and perspectives. Holding your nose while trying new foods can highlight basic tastes and textures, and planning a democratic meal where everyone chooses an item, no matter how unusual, can create bizarre yet stimulating associations. Actively engage your memory by eating foods that evoke childhood memories, or recreating a first meal with a loved one. Introduce novelty by eating meals in a different order (dessert first!), in a different location, or by using your non-dominant hand. Spice up your setting with candlelight, flowers, or music to create a multisensory experience. Introduce exotic foods and cuisines, like a Japanese breakfast or Moroccan dinner, and accompany them with ethnic music. For a unique challenge, close your eyes and identify food by smell, taste, and touch, or host a blind wine tasting. Cooking from scratch engages all senses and planning skills. Finally, consider a sexy meal with a loved one, incorporating sensory enhancements for an erotic and stimulating experience.
